title: Too early to test?
objective: For suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome (including AIDP), use electrodiagnosis early to support the diagnosis: in the first week absent H-reflexes and polyneuropathy-pattern conduction changes support it, a sural-sparing pattern is less sensitive but more specific, a normal first-week study does not exclude it, and a repeat study later helps because abnormalities can take weeks to develop

brief.situation: 11:00 in an outpatient electrodiagnostic lab. You are the physical therapist electrophysiologist. Mr. Reyes, 45, was referred by a neurologist for 'nerve conduction studies and EMG, query GBS'. The front desk booked him for three weeks from now because 'it's too early to see anything', but a cancellation brought him in today, four days after his symptoms started.
handover: He drove himself in; his wife is in the waiting room.
Lab policy: findings that suggest an acute, progressing neuropathy are phoned to the referring physician before the patient leaves.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.modelAnswer: Day 4, H-reflexes gone, polyneuropathy pattern, sural spared. That supports GBS. Even a normal study this early wouldn't have ruled it out.

scoring.modelReasoning: For suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome, electrodiagnosis is used early to support the diagnosis. In the first week absent H-reflexes and polyneuropathy-pattern conduction changes support it; sural sparing is less sensitive but more specific; a normal first-week study does not exclude it; and a repeat later helps because abnormalities can take weeks to develop. GBS is watched for progressing weakness and breathing complications, so a climbing weakness goes to the neurologist before he leaves.

earlyQ.explain: A normal first-week study does not exclude GBS; a repeat study later helps.
